segments.text: Welcome to this tutorial on IM policies
and defining permissions. In this video,
we'll learn how to write JSo policies
for fine-grained access control in AWS.
IM policies are the foundation of
security in Amazon Web Services,
allowing you to precisely control who
can access what resources and what
actions they can perform. By the end of
this tutorial, you'll understand the
structure of IM policies and how to
create your own custom policies to
secure your AWS environment.
IM policies are JSo documents that
define permissions for AWS resources and
actions. These policies are written in
JSo format, which is a standard data
interchange format that's easy to read
and write. Policies control access to
AWS services by specifying what actions
are allowed or denied on specific
resources. They can be attached to
users, groups or roles, making them
flexible and reusable. Most importantly,
IM policies enable the principle of
least privilege access, meaning you
grant only the permissions necessary for
users to perform their tasks, nothing
more.
Every M policy follows a standard JSo
structure with core elements. The
version element specifies the policy
language version and you should always
which is the current version. The
statement element is an array that
contains one or more permission
statements. Each statement must include
an effect element that specifies whether
to allow or deny access. The action
element defines which API operations are
permitted or restricted. Finally, the
resource element specifies the target a
WS resources using Amazon resource names
or a RNS. Understanding this structure
is crucial for writing effective IM
policies.
The effect element is a required
component of every M policy statement
and can have only two possible values.
When you set effect to allow, you're
granting explicit permission to perform
the specified actions on the specified
resources. Conversely, when you set
effect to deny, you're explicitly
blocking access to those actions
regardless of any other permissions.
It's important to note that deny always
overrides allow. This means if a user
has an allow statement for an action,
but also has a deny statement for the
same action, the deny takes precedence
and access is blocked.
The action element specifies which AWS
API operations are allowed or denied by
the policy. You can specify a single
action such as S3 col get object for
retrieving objects from S3. For multiple
actions, you use a JSo array with
commaepparated values like S3 get object
and S3 colon put object. Actions support
wild card patterns. So S3 colon asterisk
means all S3 actions. You can even use a
single asterisk to represent all actions
across all AWS services. Though this is
generally not recommended for security
reasons. Each action corresponds to a
specific AP I call in a WS.
The resource element specifies which AWS
resources the policy applies to using
Amazon resource names or a RNS. For
example, to target a specific S3 bucket,
you use an a rn like a rn colon a ws s3
colon my dashbucket/aststerisk.
The asterisk at the end means all
objects within that bucket. You can
specify multiple resources using a JSo
array allowing you to grant permissions
to several buckets or resources at once.
For Dynamodeb tables, the RN includes
the region and table name. While you can
use an asterisk to represent all
resources, it's best practice to be as
specific as possible to maintain proper
security controls.
The condition element is an optional but
powerful component that enables fine
grained access control. Conditions allow
you to specify circumstances under which
a policy statement is in effect. Common
condition operators include string
equals for exact text matching, date
greater than for timebased restrictions,
IP address for network-based controls,
and bool for true or false checks. In
this example, we're using the IP address
operator to restrict access to requests
coming from a specific IP address range
and a bool operator to require
multiffactor authentication.
Conditions are essential when you need
to implement advanced security controls
like restricting access based on time of
day, source IP address, or whether MFA
is enabled.
The principal element is used in
resource-based policies to specify who
can access the resource. You can specify
a specific IM user by providing their
full ON which includes the account
number and username. To grant access to
an entire AWS account, you simply
provide the 12digit account number. For
AWS services, you use the service key
with the services domain name like ec2.
Amazon aws.com.
You can even use an asterisk to make a
resource publicly accessible. Though
this should be done with extreme caution
as it allows anyone on the internet to
access the resource. The principal
element is not used in identity based
policies only in resource-based policies
like S3 bucket policies.

example that grants readonly access to a
specific S3 bucket. The policy starts
with the version element set to
The statement array contains one
statement object. The effect is set to
allow granting permission. The action is
s3 col get object which allows
downloading objects from the bucket. The
resource element specifies the exact
bucket using its an with an asterisk
indicating all objects within that
bucket. This simple but effective policy
allows a user to read objects from the
mybucket s3 bucket but prevents them
from uploading, deleting or modifying
any objects.
IM policies can contain multiple
statements to combine different
permissions in a single policy document.
In this example, we have two separate
statements within the same policy. The
first statement grants both get object
and put object permissions on an S3
bucket, allowing the user to both read
and write objects. The second statement
grants get item permission on a Dynamob
table named users, allowing read access
to that specific table. Each statement
is independent and evaluated separately.
This approach keeps related permissions
organized within a single policy
document, making it easier to manage and
audit. You can have as many statements
as needed in a single policy, though
it's best to keep them logically
organized.
This example demonstrates fine-grained
access control using conditions to add
multiple layers of security. The policy
allows all EC2 actions indicated by EC2
colon asterisk. However, access is
restricted by two conditions. First, the
IP address condition ensures that
requests must originate from a specific
IP address range. In this case,
Second, the bool condition requires that
multiffactor authentication must be
present and set to true. This means even
if a user has valid credentials and is
connecting from the allowed IP range,
they still need to authenticate with M
FA to perform EC2 actions. This layered
approach significantly enhances security
by combining multiple verification
factors.
Let's review the best practices for
writing IM policies. Always apply the
principle of least privilege by granting
only the minimum permissions necessary
for users to complete their tasks. Use
specific resources and actions rather
than broad wild cards whenever possible.
Avoid using wild cards for resources,
especially the asterisk that grants
access to all resources, as this creates
security risks. Regularly review and
audit your policies to ensure they still
align with your security requirements
and remove unnecessary permissions. Use
conditions to implement fine- grain
control based on factors like IP
addresses, time of day, or MFA status.
Finally, always test your policies using
the AM policy simulator before deploying
them to production. This tool helps you
verify that policies work as intended
and don't inadvertently grant or deny
unexpected access.
